examples: Keep every agent in view while you work in one of them.
Glance at the stats bar to see how many agents are working or waiting to be read and how many tokens are flowing, without opening anything.
how_to: Every session is listed, grouped, with its light, name and folder.
Click a row to open it; use the three dots or a right click for its actions; F2 renames it; drag it, or press alt and an arrow, to move it; search at the top.

A row's menu shows each item's key at the right end, and pressing it while the menu is open runs that item, with the same letters as every other menu: r rename, n new session in the folder, c colour, b load blueprint; any other item takes the first free letter of its name, never d or v, which stay delete and archive.

A project heading's three dots lead with new agent, which opens the same select-provider picker every other launch uses, then starts the agent in that project once you choose one; a row's add to files it into a group or a Layout, and a group's or Layout's add pulls agents in.
Show path, in a session row's menu or a project heading's menu, opens a small popup with that session's working folder (or the project folder) in full, with a copy button.
Drag its right edge to resize it; it docks beside the page on a wide screen.
A row shows small icons for what it has: agents running, background shells open, and live timers; hover one for the count and detail. Turn any of the three on or off per density in settings.

A sleeping session wears a sleep icon, an archived one an archive icon, and an inactive project a dashed folder icon after its name; hover one for its name. The show archived tick in the view menu lists every archived session and every inactive project.

When a session's Claude Code is out of date, its three-dot menu turns green: click it for update and restart on top, or shift-click the icon to jump straight to the restart confirm. It is disabled, with a reason, while the session has a running sub-agent, an open shell or a live timer.

When a session's transcript shows an MCP server dropped (an app restart drops them all until reconnected), its three-dot menu turns into a yellow exclamation; hover it for the servers, and pick reconnect mcp (key z) to type the reconnect into the session. It only works while the session is idle and is refused while it is busy. A drop shows after the session's next transcript write, since an idle session writes nothing.
A small pulsing blue workflow mark beside a row's provider icon means that session has a Workflow run going right now; it clears when the run finishes.

SysOp sits at the very top of the list, each company's agent first under its company heading and each project's agent first in its project, marked by a rank insignia (one chevron for a project leader, two for a company leader, a star for SysOp). Rename a leader with F2 or its row menu; closing, deleting or turning one off asks you to type its exact name first.

Cozy shows each agent as a meter: the first line ends in the row's controls with no figure at its right (the thin bar along the row's bottom edge is the context readout), then a second line with its model and, only while something runs, live work as counts (agents running of launched, shells, the next timer), with the model effort at the right end of that line. Detailed is a triage stack: the state word on the first line, every active flag on its own line loudest first (waiting on your permission, host unreachable, process exited, update ready, context 80% or more), then its live work. Compact is unchanged.

The row detail menu ends in show archived: on, each archived session is listed under its project after the project's other rows, drawn asleep with an archived badge, and the search finds it; waking one restarts it, which brings it back. An archived project is listed under its company too, its heading marked archived. Off, archived sessions stay out of the list and the search. The choice follows you to every device.

Click a sleeping agent and a small wake button appears in the middle of its row with an X at the right to cancel; press wake to wake it, or press the X, Escape or tap elsewhere to leave it asleep. (If you turned on wake a sleeping session straight from a click in settings, the click wakes it with no button.) On a phone the drawer now reaches to a thin strip at the right edge; tap the strip to close it.

Hold shift and click a company, project or other heading to open or close everything underneath it at once; the chevron turns into a double chevron while shift is held. Shift+Enter does the same from the keyboard.

Folds (including the providers panel) and row density are kept separately for the desktop and the phone: on a screen 700 pixels wide or less the drawer is the phone's, and what you fold or pick there does not move the desktop's. Pins and order are shared by every device.

A project has no color until you pick one. Press a project heading's kebab and pick a swatch in its color row to set the project's color, or the crossed swatch at the start of the row to remove it; the swarm list's project header takes it at once.

Click the rate to cycle per second, minute, hour and day; click the small chart to cycle the last hour, 5 hours, day and 7 days (hatched slots were not measured). It says stats off or stats paused when that is the case. On a phone it scrolls away with the search row. Both choices are kept per browser. When the feed cannot be read it says so by name (sign in for stats, stats not on this install, stats not readable) instead of waiting. A longer window folds several minutes into each bar, and hovering a bar names the span it covers. If a paired computer is paused, off or unreachable, a hatched band marks the part of the chart that undercounts, in the danger color when it cannot be reached, and a small square beside the rate shows the same at any width.
The stats bar wears no box and shows no hover tips: the counts sit on the left and the token rate sits flush right, with at most one decimal (4.5M).

Untick "show stats" in the view menu to hide the counts and token bar under the tabs; hidden, it is not drawn and does not read the stats feed. On by default, kept separately for the desktop and the phone.
Project, company, group and layout colors are drawn whenever one is set. Pick one from the heading's menu (swatches or any custom color).
Its heading folds like the others. The pinned heading shows no status light, folded or not.

Drag a section heading (pinned, layouts, groups, companies, rogue agents, terminals, browsers, pack) to put the sections in any order; on a phone drag from the little icon at the heading's left, and the rest of the heading still scrolls. A focused heading moves one slot with alt plus the up or down arrow. Escape cancels a drag. The order is the same on every device, and a section added later joins at its usual place until you move it.

Every group you made sits under one groups heading, built like layouts: click it to fold all the groups out of the way, and each group keeps its own fold, color and members. Drag a group's heading, or press alt plus the up or down arrow on it, to reorder the groups among themselves; drag the groups heading to move the whole block. While you drag a session row the groups heading stays open so every group is a drop target. Shift+click it to fold or open every group at once.

The view menu (the three bars button) has show open sessions and show sleeping sessions, both ticked by default. Open lists your awake sessions and sleeping lists your asleep ones; they are independent, so untick one to hide that set, and with both unticked no awake or sleeping session shows. Show archived and show closed sessions are unticked by default. All are kept per device, so your phone can differ from your desktop.
Right-click a project, company or group heading for the same menu its three dots open; every menu closes when you click away, and only one is open at a time.
Terminals and browsers always have a heading; empty, each says no terminals open or no browsers open. An agent's own shell lists under terminals with its folder.

A group you made with no sessions in it is not drawn (it also hides when the view's filters leave it no row, such as sleeping members with sleeping hidden), and it returns the moment a session is in it. While you drag a row every group shows so you can drop into an empty one. The group itself stays saved.
The view menu's hide empty sections tick, off by default, also hides the terminals and browsers headings while they hold nothing; a drag still shows them.

Type in the search box and the list becomes two sections: AGENTS (every agent whose name, project or folder holds the text, asleep ones included even when show sleeping is off; a pinned agent is listed once, the match is in the accent, and each row offers open session and look around, with its three dots for the rest) and the top CONVERSATIONS (saved conversation hits, each with read around, go to session or resume, copy link and more). Under the box, similar terms from your saved conversations show from 2 letters: arrow down enters them, left and right move, enter takes one, escape goes back to the box. Enter opens the highlighted result. Starting a drag keeps the text.

In the pack section, click a computer to switch it off: its agents and projects leave the list and its row dims with the name struck through; click it again to bring them back. Every computer starts on, and a phone keeps its own switches.

catalog.description: A one line, plain english label of what each live claude or codex session is working on, so a glance at a terminal head tells you what the session is for. It is made by an ai model you route for it alone (it never borrows your chat default), and it is part of the working-on labels plugin, which is off until you turn it on, refreshed when a turn ends and again while a long turn keeps working, never on a timer at idle. examples: Eight agents are open: the line above each prompt bar reminds you which one was fixing the restart picker and which one was porting the settings screen.
You answered a string of yes and continue prompts, so the last prompt says nothing; the line still names the task and its goal.

Finish a turn in any claude or codex session: the line updates on every open browser within about ten seconds, with no reload.
Click the line (or focus it and press enter) to refresh it now.

Click [hide] at the right end of the line to turn the summary off for every browser and stop its model calls, and use the session working on line switch in settings, ai, summaries to bring it back; while no model is picked the line is a link that opens settings there.
Read what the live label cost (last hour and last 24 hours) in settings, ai summaries, and set its token budget there; when it is spent, summaries pause and the panel says when they resume.

examples: The Local server and a test machine are both unreachable while conversations close: a red badge appears on the bell beside the Carnivore mark in the agents drawer, a card says no summary server reachable, and the panel shows how many summaries are waiting. You already know a server is down: dismiss the alert and it stays quiet until the condition clears, or snooze it for an hour.
You want a Slack message when the save pipeline stops, but no pop-up card: tick save pipeline under the Slack destination and untick it on screen.
how_to: Click the bell beside the Carnivore mark in the agents drawer (or under the claw of the closed drawer's icon rail): open alerts first, errors before warnings, each with its count and first and last seen; resolved alerts of the last 24 hours fold underneath. On a phone with the drawer shut, a coloured dot on the claw says an alert is open; tap the claw, then the bell. Clicking any alert card opens the panel too.
Dismiss, snooze 1h, or clear resolved from the panel; each is a route: POST /api/v1/alerts/{id}/dismiss, POST /api/v1/alerts/{id}/snooze {minutes}, POST /api/v1/alerts/dismiss-resolved.
GET /api/v1/alerts?state=active|all for the list and the badge counts; changes also arrive on /ws/events as app_alert.raised, app_alert.updated and app_alert.resolved.
An alert card can be hidden per type: untick that alert's row in the screen column of the routing matrix. The bell and the panel still list it.

Alerts can also be routed to outside destinations (chat, push, email, sms): tick the alert rows (self check, save pipeline, archive, transcripts, account, phone link) under a destination in the matrix.

catalog.description: One time zone for the whole app. Repeating schedules in the task manager (every day at 09:00, weekdays at 09:00, monthly on the 1st) are read in it. It is new york until you pick another, it is saved on the server so every device and every agent sees the same one, and an agent can read and change it with the preferences tools.
examples: You moved to Paris: pick Europe/Paris and your daily 09:00 stand-up repeat comes due at 09:00 Paris time from its next run on.
A one-time reminder set for Friday 15:00 New York time still fires at that exact moment after you change the zone; only repeating wall times are re-read.
An agent asked to schedule a daily 08:30 check reads the zone with preferences_get (time_zone) so it knows whose 08:30 that is.
how_to: Open settings, general, time zone. Type part of a name (paris, new york, tokyo) in the search box and click the zone in the list; it saves at once.
To go back to new york, pick America/New_York, or have an agent send preferences_update with time_zone null.
Agents: preferences_get returns time_zone (absent means America/New_York); preferences_update with {"time_zone": "Europe/Paris"} changes it. A name this server does not know is refused.

A restarted session stops on claude's new MCP server approval (or the resume picker, the bypass warning, or a screen nobody has seen before): a read-only card names the session and shows the screen text; clicking it opens the session, and the card goes away once claude starts.
how_to: Open the questions tab in the drawer (it shows only while something is waiting) or click the notification: each card names the session and project, shows the question and its options. Click an option to answer; multi-select cards have checkboxes and submit; a free text row has a text box.

Turn the cross-session mcp gate on or off under settings, sessions and agents, hold cross-session agent actions. It is off by default.
GET /api/v1/approvals for the list; POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/dialog/answer {fingerprint, choice} to answer; the approvals frame on /ws/events says when to re-read.

catalog.description: The Automations page lists them with their next fire time, newest run and an on or off switch; edit, run now and delete sit on each row. Cron also reads the third Tuesday style, written 2#3 in the day-of-week field, and POST /automations/schedule/parse turns a sentence like every third Tuesday at 5 PM into a cron through the connected AI, for confirmation only. The editor checks the cron as you type and shows the next five fires or the reason it is refused (two fires under 15 minutes apart, or never). catalog.description: A mod is a Claude Code plugin that changes how Claude Code looks and behaves; it is code that runs with your permissions and is not sandboxed. catalog.description: The crate plugin writes a session or a project, its conversations, their side files and Carnivore's own records into one file. An own crate is byte exact and never redacted; it is fully verified before it is kept, recorded as an export (deep search tags each conversation), and copied and verified at an optional second folder. Encryption is optional and standard age v1 to the public keys in the plugin's settings; the private key stays in 1Password. A share crate is separate: secrets starred, images removed, the home folder hidden, never recorded, and it resumes only as a fork. Every build reads every crate version ever written, and python3 -m src.core.crate_format verifies or extracts one offline.

catalog.description: Deep search is built into the app. Results come back one group per conversation: its session name, project and date, how many matches, and its best few hits with the match marked. A small ledger / best hits toggle in the results header picks the layout (remembered per device). The picked hit offers read around, go to session or resume, branch here, copy link (a link that reopens that message's context window), bookmark this message and only this conversation; a hit with no session or read from a backup offers read around and copy link only. The index mirrors your disk file by file: when a transcript file is deleted or moved its rows go at the next pass (unless the save plugin is on and holds it), and a second copy of the same conversation keeps its own. The index is a disposable cache file that rebuilds itself from your transcripts if it is ever deleted, and searches keep answering from the older index until the new one is complete. It is always on. The save plugin adds the backup fallback: with save off the results still show, a deleted conversation is no longer found from backup, and a line says the index is paused. With another computer paired, each computer searches its own transcripts and the results merge: a conversation held by the other computer carries a small tag with that computer's name, one held by both is listed once and says so, and a computer that did not answer is named in one quiet line instead of delaying the rest. A conversation on the other computer opens only when a live session of it is listed here; otherwise its row says which computer holds it. Agents get the same search, peer hits included and tagged, as the conversation_search tool. Agents get the window through the deepsearch_context_get tool.

catalog.description: The developer widget is a tab strip over a list of monitors. The figure columns keep the room their widest value needs, so a run time is never cut off. A narrow tab drops the area and then what ran it, never the run time, and a next run a day or more away reads in days and hours (in 6d 23h), so a weekly or monthly schedule is never cut off either. The mark before a name is a shape as well as a color: a filled circle ok, a diamond error, a dash skipped. A global / sessions / both switch on top picks Carnivore's automations (global), the huddle's scheduled task items with their next fire (sessions, read only while the task manager plugin is on; with it off the sessions view says so), or both; the choice is remembered in this browser. Who pressed run now is kept in the run's own notes when the button is pressed (no new column). The scheduled tab updates from the server's pushes (the automations and automation runs topics, and the huddle's list topic), and the pipeline tab from the pipeline topic, with no timed polling while the live connection is up; only the selected tab reads anything, and the chosen tab is remembered in this browser. The selected tab is the lighter fill and the other tabs the darker one. A new monitor is one entry in the widget's monitor list. It updates from the server's pushes with no polling at idle, and with the Task Manager plugin off it still shows the copies kept in this browser. It reads records, not lines: a Python traceback or stderr text stays with the event it follows, its line count shows on the row in the danger color and opening the row shows the whole record as JSON with the traceback under it. A strip on top has one toggle for each level (error, warn, info, debug), all on at first and remembered in this browser, one chip per source, the server's log level (changed live, or back to the .env value), export (the records shown, as a .jsonl download) and clear. Under it a text filter (write /pattern/ for a regular expression) and a session filter that matches any of the ways the log names a session. Click a field on a row to show only that value, Alt-click to hide it; each active field filter is a chip you click to remove. Load older pages back through the file and its rotated copies. Secrets are masked again before anything is shown. It updates from the server's pushes with no polling at idle.

A removed widget stays in the drawer and drags back with its settings. Every change is saved the way that screen already saves: the home screen on this browser, a session's terminal page synced to every device. catalog.description: Carnivore connects to a messaging provider (the imsg bridge, speaking the Carnivore Provider Protocol) and binds sessions to conversations, in, out or both. A text from you reaches the bound session: a threaded reply goes to the session that sent the original, a leading @name to that session, otherwise the default one; with several bound and none named, Carnivore texts back which session. Only your own handles, as imessage, are accepted; an sms gets a short reply asking for imessage, and a stranger gets nothing. While a permission, question or startup dialog is open the text is held and you get one text saying so; it goes in when the dialog closes, and several held texts arrive as one batch, oldest first, each dated. An asleep session is woken. An edit or unsend replaces or drops a held text, and sends a short note after delivery. A bound session sends with messaging_send: text only, secrets starred, rate limited, and logged first. Secrets live in the keychain only, and the provider's address is write-only.
examples: You text restart the feed while the session is asking a permission question; you get held for ledgerbot, and the text goes in after you answer the dialog.
Three texts sent while the computer was asleep arrive as one message, oldest first, each with its time and age.

On the provider, press add conversation and add the conversation with you; only conversations the bridge lists as routable can be added.
Ask an agent with the messaging tools to bind the session to the conversation (it names a direction: in and out, in only or out only); you approve the bind when it asks.
Text the conversation from your phone. Start with @name to reach one session when several are bound, or reply to a session's own text.
Watch the log on the settings screen for held and failed messages; retry a failed one there.
A text you sent whose outcome is unknown (the bridge restarted mid-send) shows in the log as unconfirmed, in its own color, with no retry: check your phone before sending it again.
On the provider card, the duplicate-send protection line says whether a retried send was ever answered with the original result (proven, with when) or never seen yet.

catalog.description: Twelve kinds of destination, many instances of each: slack, discord, microsoft teams (workflows webhook), telegram, ntfy, pushover, a generic signed webhook, email (smtp), sms through aws sns, sms through twilio, pagerduty, and every web push device. Every secret, recipient and number lives in the Keychain and is write-only. One matrix lists 29 notification types in families (needs you, sessions, accounts, health, app, in-app only) against a screen column plus one column per destination. Every cell can be unticked, needs-you included; needs-you starts ticked. Hiding a card hides the pop-up only: the bell, the history, the status light and the tray keep everything. Each destination can add away mode, quiet hours, a reminder and a project filter, and can opt in to details (tool and target, or the question snippet; scrubbed, capped at 200 characters, never on sms). The message carries a link back, tried in order: the mobile sync public address, then the local name, then the network address, then no link. A pause switch holds all outside delivery on one computer. Settings and secrets sync to paired computers over the paired link, secrets landing in each computer's Keychain; any tick or destination can be pinned to one computer. An agent can send you a notification with the notify tool. The old Slack, ntfy and Pushover secrets move into the Keychain.
examples: You walk away from your desk: the permission and question notifications go to your phone through ntfy or Pushover, and a quiet-hours window keeps the finished-turn pings off at night while a permission request still gets through.
A shared channel gets a Slack message when a session dies, but with details off, so no command or file name leaves the computer.
Your laptop and your desktop are paired: add a destination once and it appears on both, with its secret stored in each computer's Keychain.
A destination fails five times in a row with a permanent error: it is switched off and a notifications health alert tells you, without that alert being sent outside.
how_to: Open settings, notifications, destinations, press add a destination, pick a kind from the grouped list (each service has its logo; click the field or use the arrow keys, type to filter), fill in its fields and press add. Secrets are write-only: once saved they show as set, and a blank field keeps the stored one. A webhook generates a signing secret for you and shows it once.
Press test on a destination to send one fixed test message; one test every 10 seconds.

Open settings, notifications, routing. Tick a notification under a destination to send it there. The screen column decides which cards pop up; needs-you rows start ticked and can be unticked like any other. A tick on the new destination column sets what a new destination starts with.
Press reset to global on a pinned cell to go back to the synced value.

Under routing, read the link line: it says which link outside messages carry (mobile sync address, local name, network address or none) and why.

An agent in a session can call the notify tool to send you one notification of type agent.message, routed by the matrix. The switch is mcp.agent_notify (PUT /api/v1/mcp-admin/agent-notify); off hides the tool.

catalog.description: The Swarm page opens from the swarm page link on the drawer's huddle panel (or the #swarm link) and leaves the drawer on its tab. All three show the same active floor, with one quiet link to show the inactive ones, and all three follow the node filter, which shows one node's lineage: the node, its parents up to SysOp and everything under it. An agent's chat groups its messages in bursts: one header per run from the same sender (an arrow in for what the agent received, out for what it sent, the sender's square, its path and the time since), follow-ups tucked under it with only a dim time, two or more quiet events in a row folded into one "N events" line that opens in place, and a question or review card always under its own header with a yellow edge; an outgoing crosstalk message is headed by the agent it went to. A click on an agent anywhere (a ledger row, a node, a square, a name in a chat message, an agent row in the huddle) opens its chat with its terminal beside it, on the right (at 1024 px and wider the chat docks and the terminal moves over; a press in that terminal keeps the chat open; the swarm page steps aside); an asleep agent opens its chat alone and is never woken by the click. A company or project with no agent is a vacant seat that asks before turning one on. The settings tab picks the default view, the default density and the character set. Project, company and SysOp nodes wear the same rolled-up status the Agents tab heading shows, and a vacant seat takes that status's hue on its dashed outline. Every project, company and SysOp wears its own bright color, as unlike the others as the screen allows on the theme you are using (each new one picked as the color farthest from every one before it, so adding one never moves the rest; dark and light themes get their own sets, neons and near-whites included), and only a project's agents and sessions share its tone, each a distinct bright shade, never a muddy one; a color you set by hand on an agent still wins. Its settings tab also sets the Swarm look for every device: agent colors by project or random, a body shape per agent type and an animation per status.

catalog.description: A send does one of three things on a paired computer. Move is the session move: the agent stops here and continues there with its conversation. Copy waits for the current turn to end, carries a whole-lines snapshot of the conversation and starts a new session there that resumes it as a fork with its own conversation id, while the original keeps running untouched; the code keeps syncing both ways: when either agent finishes a turn its new commits go to the other computer, which fast-forwards its checked-out branch only when its agent is idle, its tree is clean and the move is a pure fast-forward. Fresh starts a new agent in the same project on that computer with no conversation. When the other computer does not hold the project yet, with_project adds it as a replica and syncs it first; without that the refusal stays project_not_on_target. The other computer decides every refusal by its own restrictions. A check route reports per mode what would work, with no side effects, and progress is a pack op. Before you confirm, the send dialog shows a plain checklist: what comes along, what stays behind and why (uncommitted work, ignored folders with their size, another project's folders), tools the conversation ran that the other computer lacks, and servers that will stop. Folders outside the project that the agent used are read from the conversation since its last compaction; a computer that cannot take them yet says to update it.

catalog.description: It is global only, off the surface until you place it, and it draws the new engine. Hovering a square, focusing it with the keyboard or tapping it opens its detail: how many files wait and how old the oldest is, when it last delivered, its last error and how many are failing, and how many runs since the server started. The overall status line (caught up, behind, stalled, rebuilding or off) sits small beside the row. The engine announces a delivery when it starts as well as when the batch ends, so running shows without polling. A failed run wears a diamond mark, a parked one a dash. Every figure column keeps the room its widest value needs, so the run time is never cut off; the name and area give way first, and a very narrow widget drops the runs and then the area before any figure. The server keeps these rows in memory only (about 100, empty after a restart); it records and logs, it never alerts. Every view shares one read of GET /api/v1/pipeline/status, pushed on the pipeline topic after every batch, park, scan pass and rebuild, so nothing polls while the live connection is up (a 10 second poll runs only while it is down). The developer widget carries it as its pipeline tab. While the conversation backups plugin is on, the chart also shows a backups row (area conversations, #1807): its 30 minute passes plus the captures on close, sleep, restart, clear and fork as runs, the last run's time and duration, and a failed mark when the latest pass or capture failed; with the plugin off the row is not there. It comes through a plugin seam (src/cplugs/sdk/pipeline_rows.py), so the plugin stays self contained.

catalog.description: Every plugin built into this app, on the shared manager frame, one kind of row with one switch each. A plugin that is switched off stops contributing to every surface it adds to (the session row menu, a tab, a menu link). Mark unread and share read only are plugins that ship on; huddle ships on for a clean install and keeps an existing install's choice. The choice is stored on the server, so every device agrees. Built-in plugins are part of the app, so none of those can be installed or removed here. Store plugins from the catalog sit on the same page as the same card warez draws (hero image on top, same order as warez): a plugin that is not installed shows the same add control as warez (add, with its caret to pick global or a project), a plugin with an update due shows update, and only an installed plugin shows its switch, which turns it off for the picked project. A plugin that runs a program (an MCP server) prints the full command on its card; add goes through warez's one-click route and opens the install sheet when the server asks for consent. Turning one on grants what it asks, listed in its details. The details are tabbed: overview, settings, permissions and data, with the state and switch always at the top and a plain reason when a plugin is held or waiting for a grant. Each permission is shown by risk tier, a plugin that asks for something dangerous in combination carries a warning, and a plugin's recent permission use is listed in its details. An agent can turn a plugin off or revoke grants over MCP, never turn one on or add a grant.

catalog.description: The review board is a plugin (off by default, needs the huddle) for mockups that go through rounds of review. A board is one folder in a git checkout: a sidecar file and one immutable page per revision, so the folder alone rebuilds the board. The read side is: the boards folder setting (it must be a real folder holding a .boards-root file, inside a git checkout, and never the app copy, an app bundle or the app state folder), the list of boards with whose turn each is in (your turn, with claude, undelivered), one board in full with the rounds you sent word for word, a rescan after a hand edit or a git pull, and two agent tools to read them. The board page shows a board read only: a title strip with whose turn it is, a history bar of revisions with the rounds you sent as diamonds between them, and the mockup itself in a locked-down frame (scripts run, but it has no network, storage or login, and it can only point at tagged parts of the page). You can step through revisions, switch between the real width and a fit-to-width view, and pop the page out into a tab of its own. Claude opens a board on your screen with task_manager_board_focus. Claude publishes boards and revisions: task_manager_board_create starts a board for a task and task_manager_board_revision_add adds each next revision (a page, a summary and the prompts to answer); every revision posts a card on the task and by default puts the task in review. A revision's files are never changed once written, and a failed write leaves the board as it was. A revision may instead own its controls (payload_mode): the page posts its state, the board header has a draft light, a save stepper, a note for the agent and send, there is no sidebar, the page's state autosaves as one overwriting draft, every send makes a numbered save and only nudges the session to review the payload, and a theme picker repaints just the page in another Carnivore theme. Closed reviews: a board whose task is done is closed (derived on read, never stored, so reopening the task reopens it), and each project's page on the projects page has a closed reviews group listing them, newest closed first, while the plugin is on. A revision may also name a questions layer (task_manager_board_create and task_manager_board_revision_add take layer): claude sends a list of questions instead of writing the controls, and the board draws them inside the frame, with no page needed. The fields are yes or no, pick one, pick several, on or off, a short text and a long text, and each question has a small note key. Questions sit right under the part of the page they ask about, the rest in one section at the end, or all in one panel at the edge of the frame (a bottom sheet on a phone). Your answers autosave, step through saves and send exactly like a payload page, and arrive as values and notes keyed by the question ids.

catalog.description: An agent can bring a left bar item into view for you. The tool sidebar_show takes a kind (session, file, browser, board, layout or task_manager) and an id, checks the item exists, and shows it in the window you used last, the one with your latest click or key press. If you have not used any window since the app started, or every window has closed, there is nothing to show it in, and the agent is told so. A window you close is forgotten, so the show falls back to the window you used before it. In the desktop app the window that gets the item also comes to the front.

catalog.description: Skill scout, in a session's session skills panel, pastes a short request into the running Claude agent. catalog.description: The board tab on the Swarm page shows every Swarm card in five views behind one switcher: swimlanes, list, timeline, calendar and columns by project. Swimlanes is the default. Swimlanes draws one lane per project (or named list) with a full-width header: the project name, its company, its card total, how many are done, the faces of the agents working its cards and a stacked bar of todo, in progress, review and done. An open lane shows its todo, in progress, review and done cards side by side in faintly tinted columns, five per cell with a +N more key; a card shows its number, age, title, a one-line summary of what it is for, who holds it, a working, queued, paused or stalled chip and its reported progress as a calm green bar. Click a card to open the same detail pane the list view uses. Drag a card to reorder its queue (the order agents are dealt cards) or into another column: in progress to todo pauses it, into done completes it. Each card carries quick action keys for its stage: top and bottom, pause, mark done, auto-promote for a todo card, reclassify with a note for the next agent, archive (the archived key brings it back), collapse to one line and delete with a confirm. Agents hear about a move about 15 seconds after the last change, so a quick undo never reaches them. A lane with nothing in progress or in review is folded to one line with its four counts, and your own fold or unfold is remembered on this device. Filter by scope (sysop, a company or a project), all cards or only yours, and search by #number or title. The board updates by itself when any card changes, and the device remembers the view you picked. The list view puts every card not yet done in three bands, the cards waiting on your review first under needs you, then in progress, then todo, each child right under its parent. Click a row to open its detail pane: the created, started, review and done steps with their times, its progress, result and how to validate it, its history newest first, and done or send back with a note, which mark the card through the same routes as everywhere else. The calendar view shows the week (or today, or the last three days) as a grid: one row per project grouped by company, and in each day how many of its cards were created, started, sent to review, approved or sent back, an hourly activity bar under it, the faces of the agents whose card started that day, a now line in today, hatched days still to come and a key at the bottom. The timeline view draws the last twelve hours (or three days, or a week) on a time scale: per project, each parent card as a thick bar with its children nested under it and a dashed link where each child reached review, then the cards with no parent. A bar shows waiting, working and review spans, grey where the start was never recorded; the working agent's face sits on every bar being worked and on its parent's line, a now line crosses every lane and the shared key sits at the bottom. The columns by project view puts each project in its own column with its cards stacked under its name, the ones waiting on your review first, then in progress, todo and done, five of each before a +N more key; each card carries its state glyph, the same quick action keys and opens the same detail pane, and a todo or queued card drags to a new place in its queue.

catalog.description: The first slice of the swarm cards work. A card is a huddle task: nothing is copied and no task row is rewritten. Its board column is worked out from its state, who holds it, whether claude is working it and whether the agent that made it accepted the report: todo, in progress, review or done. The huddle database gains the card columns and tables in one migration that writes no rows, and the server takes a checked copy of the database (huddle.db.pre-cards plus the time) before it runs. One writer in the huddle plugin owns every card change, and a test fails if any other file writes a card column. A new cards push topic tells open browsers to re-read the board. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.

catalog.description: The second slice of the swarm cards work. Spawning an agent gives it a card (the one you name, or one made from its goal). A card holder's report goes through the same finish path and is tied to the card, so accepting the report accepts the card; when the last child card of a parent is accepted the parent moves to Review with every child's steps merged. catalog.description: The third slice of the swarm cards work: dealing and leases. When cards enter a project's Todo queue, the server sends the project agent one deal request after a 5 second window, however many cards arrived, and wakes it if it sleeps. The request lists the top of the queue and the free agents, and stays open until the agent deals a card or answers with hold; an unanswered request is sent again after 15 minutes, three times in all, then a line in the chat tells you. Dealing is off for every project that existed when this shipped: turn it on per project with the dealing switch (a project made later starts on). A card an agent holds in progress carries a lease: 10 minutes with no card write, no busy reading and no stop reading hands it back for a new deal (the old agent is told to stop and the next agent starts from the handoff note), or, with dealing off, marks it stalled with one line in the chat. An open question, a permission or dialog on screen, or a pause stops the clock; a plain session's working claim never lapses. A working agent whose handoff note is half an hour old is asked once to refresh it. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.

A card held by an agent that has shown no sign of life for ten minutes goes back to Todo marked handed off, and the project agent is asked to deal it again; with dealing off it stays with the agent, marked stalled, and the chat says it is waiting for you.

catalog.description: The fourth slice of the swarm cards work: the capacity governor. A card dealt to an agent that has no body yet (asleep) needs a new body, and the governor decides whether that may start now. It waits when the project has no free slot (a project or company with no grant has no limit of its own since #1439, and you or SysOp can grant 0 to 20 per project or company; while a project is throttled for merge conflicts it runs at most 3), or when the machine is hot: the CPU has been over 85 percent for the last two minutes, or a fresh usage window is over 90 percent on the Claude account the new agent will run on (a different account that is parked at its limit holds nothing back; when that account cannot be told, every account counts). The capacity reading, the slot refusal, the spawn refusal and the deal request name that account and the window that tripped. A deal that waits shows the card marked waiting for a slot, and the server deals it by itself, oldest first, once a slot frees. The governor never pauses, sleeps or kills running work, never touches a card an agent already holds, and a deal to an awake agent always goes through. The governor's CPU reading is whole-machine busy time; separately, since #1439 every new agent body is admitted by measuring the machine (load average per core and free memory), and refused with system is pegged, try later and a retry_after when it cannot take one. While a project's dealing switch is off the two machine floors do not apply, so your own explicit deals are not held back by a hot machine. SysOp and company agents read the numbers with swarm_card_capacity, set grants with swarm_card_grant and set a project's pace (normal: one card per free agent, asap: use every free slot) with swarm_card_pace; the deal request the project agent receives now names its free slots, the cards waiting for one and the pace. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Grant a project 2 slots while two of its agents are running: a card dealt to a third, sleeping agent reads waiting for a slot, and starts by itself the moment one of the two finishes.
With the CPU over 85 percent for two minutes and dealing on, a deal to a sleeping agent waits; the agents already working are not touched, and the card is dealt when the machine cools.

Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/grants/project:16 with slots 0 to 20 and a reason to cap a project (company:3 for a company); send slots null to go back to the default.

catalog.description: The agent side of swarm cards. A feature or task agent's brief now teaches the card loop: start the card, keep the handoff current, finish with a result and how-to-validate steps, release when stuck, and never mark a card done. A project agent's standing rules add how to run the queue: deal the top cards in order, hold when nothing should start, split big cards, accept or reject reports and suggest reorders. Every wake, fresh or resumed, repeats a short card duty. A dealt card's message lists up to three facts its chain already knows, with their ids, so what a parent learned travels down, and a spawned child's first message lists them next to its card. The huddle guide moves to revision 6 and teaches plain sessions the four columns, that a swarm-held card refuses huddle state writes, and that only you reach Done. Backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.

catalog.description: The sixth slice of the swarm cards work. Every line in an agent's conversation now carries a category (conversation, result, question, important, dealt, and so on), and card traffic lines that carry one now show in the conversation instead of being dropped. A new swarm_chat_muted preference hides categories: the conversation route takes view=shown to drop what you muted (unset shows only conversation, result, question and important), while view=all, the default, drops nothing. Your own words and the agent's can never be muted. The only thing that goes to your phone is a question that climbed to you because no agent above the asker could answer it: it is one push of its own type, swarm.question_climbed, seeded on web push and native app push only, and the question card is marked sent to your phone only when a destination actually took the push (a type left unticked, quiet hours or paused routing leave it unmarked). A swarm body's own finished, attention and posted toasts stay in the app (matched on the body's own tmux instance, so a later plain session that reuses a destroyed body's name still pushes); its permission, question and plan dialogs still go out. This slice is backend only: the chat filter UI waits for the layout pick.
examples: Mute dealt and handed_off lines with swarm_chat_muted, then read an agent's conversation with view=shown: those lines are gone and your own messages stay.

An agent asks something no one above it can answer: your web push destination gets one swarm question for you push once you tick that type on the notifications screen, and the card reads sent to your phone; with that type unticked everywhere the card stays unmarked.

catalog.description: The seventh slice of the swarm cards work. A card in Review can now be validated: the project agent starts a fresh task agent that runs the card's how-to-validate steps (through a validator agent definition when the project has one, else with its own tools) and ends with a pass or fail verdict plus the proof it saw, kept word for word on the card. A pass marks the card validated and, when the project's auto-done switch is on, moves it to Done, after re-checking inside the Done write that the pass still covers the card (a send-back and re-finish, or a newer validation run, in between keeps it in Review). A fail sends the card back to In Progress marked validation failed with the proof, held again by the agent that finished it, which is told what failed. With nothing to validate it, the card reads no proof yet and the validate route answers 409. You start a validation from the validate route, or turn on the project's auto-validate switch so every card that reaches Review is validated by itself. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: With auto-validate and auto-done both on for a project, a card that reaches Review is validated; on a pass it moves to Done by itself, and on a fail it goes back to In Progress.
how_to: Call POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/validate on a card in Review to start a validation now; it answers 409 no_capability when the project has no validator agent and no project agent.
Call GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/{card_id}/validation to read the state, the proof (null reads no proof yet), what would validate the card and whether a start would be accepted.
Call PUT /api/v1/swarm/cards/rules/{project_id} with auto_validate to validate every card that reaches Review, and auto_done to finish a card after a pass.
The validating agent ends with the swarm_card_verdict tool: card_id, verdict pass or fail, and the proof.

catalog.description: The eighth slice of the swarm cards work. A company agent (or SysOp) can now make one parent card in its own list and hang child cards on it in several of its projects' queues; each child is dealt by that project's own project agent, as any card is. Children of another company's project are refused, and a company agent adds children only under its own cards or its company's project cards. When every child, in any project, is done, the parent moves to Review by itself with a merged how-to-validate (n of n done, plus each child's steps and proof), and your Done on the parent finishes the children too. On the company and SysOp board a parent shows once in its own lane and again in the lane of every project that holds one of its children, marked as the parent of the cards in that lane. This slice is backend only: the board screen waits for the layout pick.
examples: Zeta's agent and Alpha's agent each deal their own child. When both are accepted the parent reads Review, 2 of 2 done, and shows in both project lanes on the company board.
Company 2's agent tries to hang a child in its own project under company 1's card and is refused; Alpha (SysOp) may do it anywhere.
how_to: Make the parent in the company agent's own list, then make each child with the swarm_card_create tool naming the parent and the project_id of the project it goes in.
Read GET /api/v1/swarm/cards/board?scope=company:<id> or scope=sysop; a cross-project parent has lane_role parent_of_children_here in every lane but its own.
Click Done on the parent in Review (POST /api/v1/swarm/cards/{id}/done) to finish it and its children.

catalog.description: A widget for the right widget bar (the bar the notepad lives on). Its key opens a drawer beside the terminal, sized like the notepad: drag the drawer's left edge for width and, when it shares the drawer with another widget, drag the line between them for height. One item per row, never nested, in the order questions, reviews, working, waiting, scheduled, open, the item touched last first inside a status. A row is the Task Manager's own status mark, the title and how old it is; a question wears a yellow stripe. Compact rows are one 20px line so eight or more fit; two-line rows add the latest message under the title with who wrote it. The title row carries the count and the two density keys, which show when the pointer or focus is in the row. Hover a title or second line that is cut off with an ellipsis to see all of it. Press a row to open it in place, one at a time: a question shows the Task Manager's real answer form, a review its latest line and the reply box, every other row its latest line, and each has open in task manager. Right-click the widget's key, or anywhere in the list, for the six status checks of the Task Manager's badge menu under the heading show in list; ticking keeps the menu open and the ticks are stored on that copy, so you can place it more than once with different statuses, and they sync to every device. The key's badge is the number of rows the copy lists. The list is pushed from the Task Manager's own store and never polls.
examples: Keep only questions and reviews ticked for a short list of what waits on you.
Add a second copy with only working ticked to watch what the agents are doing.

Press its key to open the drawer; drag the drawer's left edge to size it.
Right-click the key (or the list) and tick the statuses you want to see; the menu stays open.
Press a row to open it in place; a question shows the answer form.
Use the two icons in the title row to switch between compact and two-line rows.
Use the status and folder icons in the title row to group the rows under headers by status or by project; each header shows its count.

Press open in task manager on an open row: the Task Manager widget comes up (its bar opens if it was shut), the group unfolds and the task scrolls into view. With no Task Manager widget placed, a small warning says to add one from edit layout.

catalog.description: A two-way list you and claude both write to, in a tab of the left sidebar. There is one list per project and one shared all projects list. Claude adds items (done: this, need your call: that), marks them done and asks you a question on any item; you add items for claude, drag them into priority order, check the ones that are good, and leave a note where it is good but claude should read something. A checked item with a note reads good, read the note. Each item has a short thread: claude asks, you reply, and your reply answers its question. When claude posts, a notice fires and the tab's badge turns yellow while a question waits, without taking you away from the tab you are on; the tab sits in the strip while the show tab setting is on and has no close key. Tell carnivore in the tab's title row sends one line to a claude session of the project saying the list changed, picking the most recently active one or letting you choose. Claude reads only what changed through its huddle tools and can never approve, reorder or delete. The pop out key in the title row opens the huddle in its own window so it sits beside what you are working on.
examples: Claude finishes a change and adds done: the folder picker; you check it, and claude sees it is approved the next time it reads the list.
You add fix the toast colour to the project's list, drag it to the top and press tell carnivore.
Claude asks which of two names you want on an item; the swarm tab shows a yellow badge, you reply in the thread.
You ask claude what it needs from you right now; it highlights the two items waiting on your call and opens the most urgent one, in the sidebar and the pop-out alike, until you touch the list.
Claude replies on an item while you are away; when you come back the row wears the unread light and the tab badge says 1; opening the row clears it on your phone too.

While claude works on your item it adds a note on the thread: the row keeps its working stripe, shows no unread dot and gets a small yellow light until you open it; when claude wants you to look at a result the row's light turns blue and counts as unread.
Claude marks an item done and it moves into ready to review; you write a reply on it and it moves out of ready to review into open, then to working once claude reads it.
You screenshot a broken layout, paste it into the reply box and press reply; claude reads the picture from its path on the thread.
Claude flags three items purple with the reason needs a decision; you see the purple stripes and one legend entry, and the flags clear as you tick each item.

You switch the nudge on for a project (the edit project modal or the bell on its bar); an open item goes quiet for an hour, carnivore wakes that project's idle agent about it, and after three nudges with no change the item asks you to unstick it.
You reply on a task, press tell, and see sent to carnivore 14:31 then reply received 14:31 under your message; ten minutes later a bell on another task's row shows the agent never fetched your reply.
how_to: The huddle is called swarm in the app. It ships on for a clean install and stays off on an existing install until you turn it on: open the plugins page from the menu tab, find swarm (marked plugin) and press its switch, which grants what it asks.

Open the menu tab and choose swarm: the plugins page opens on the swarm plugin's side pane, at its settings (link: #plugins/huddle/settings). The show tab switch (on by default) keeps the swarm tab in the strip with no close key; switch it off to hide the tab, on any browser. The swarm look and page fields are in the same section, below the switches.
Pick a list at the top: all projects or one project.
Type in the box at the bottom and press add to give claude an item.
Drag a row by its dotted grip to change its priority, or focus the grip and press the up and down arrows.
Check a row to approve it; press the note key to add a note, which makes it good, read the note.
Click a row (or press Enter on it) to open it: the thread sits under the description, with claude's question and your reply box. A question or review row also carries its own reply box.
Paste a picture or file into a reply box, or drop files on it: each uploads at once and shows as a chip (the x removes it); send posts them with your words, or alone.

Press tell carnivore at the bottom right to tell a claude session the list changed now; your ordinary changes also go out on their own a few seconds after you stop. If the list has no session, a pop-up above the key offers start a new session, a running session, or stop.
Press the pop out key in the title row to open the huddle in its own window.
Press hide completed (the eye, icon only) in the bar to hide checked items (it stays off until you turn it on, on every device); the eye shows whether it is on, and unchecking an item brings it back.

Press the count at the far left of the bar (the number of checked items), then the red delete key, to delete the checked items of the list on screen; the confirm says they are gone for good, not hidden.
Press the lines key beside the add box to type several items at once, one per line.

Ask claude what it needs from you: it marks those tasks with one of eight solid shapes (the marker), which sit in the row's left margin; the list bar then shows a key for each shape in use, and pressing one shows only those tasks with every project and group opened.
Press the magnifier in the list bar to search tasks loosely ('rvwbrd' finds 'review board'); everything opens while you search and only matching tasks show; the clear key brings your folds back.

On a project header, press the info badge to read that project's infos in a list and dismiss them, press any other status badge to show only that status everywhere (press it again to clear), and click the project's name to fold or unfold it.

When claude wants a ticked item reopened, or an open one closed, it asks with a reason: the request waits in the approvals inbox as one card (title, current and target state, reason), nothing changes until you approve, and the answer is left as a line on the item. Closing means your approve is the tick.

The keys at the foot are icons only, with their names on hover: far left the remove completed count, then (in the by group view only) new group and show empty groups, and on the right hide completed (the eye) and tell carnivore (the arrow). The add box sits in its own strip below them.

A row with the green unread light holds something claude added, changed, answered or pointed at since you last looked; open or tick it to clear the light on every device. The tab badge and the list picker count the unread rows.

Read a row's left stripe for who it waits on: bright yellow is claude's question for you, green is claude working on it, cyan is claude done and waiting on your review, violet is built but not yet installed; hover the row number for the words.

Tell carnivore tells every changed list into its own session (from all projects, each list that changed); a list with no session to tell comes up in one pop-up where you pick a session for it. The number inside tell carnivore counts your changes not yet sent, and drops to 0 as soon as a tell sends them.

Each row shows a small status icon at its left (question, working, ready to review, waiting to install, ticked, open, todo); an info icon there means claude left a message you have not opened yet. An item with a change claude has not read yet shows as open.
Open an item to read its thread as a chat under the description: claude on the left, you on the right, in its own scroll box that opens on the newest message.
By group, each group splits into status subsections (for example, widgets: question for you); done and todo start folded.

Hide a status you do not want to see: on the list bar's right end press the funnel to open the status filter card: one icon per status the list shows. All are on and the funnel is dim; click one to hide its rows in every view, click again to show them. Your choice is remembered on this device. With anything hidden the funnel turns blue. A hidden status that still holds items waiting on you (needs you, question, ready to review) shows a red ! on its key and on the funnel.
The add box's list follows the project of the tab you are on, while the list on screen stays where you put it.

Press the folder key at the left of the control row to make a named group in the list on screen; drag a row by its grip onto a group (or its header when folded) to file it there, and back above the groups to ungroup it.
A group's header folds it (every device folds together); hover it for rename, up, down and remove. Removing a group keeps its items, ungrouped. An open item's move to key also lists the groups.
Ask claude to sort the list into groups: it makes them and files items with task_manager_group_create and the group argument of task_manager_add and task_manager_move.

Press enter in a reply box or the one-line add box to save it; the tell about that list is queued and goes out after a few quiet seconds, or when you press tell carnivore (in the multiline box enter is a new line and cmd+enter adds).

The list sorts itself by status (the default): needs you, question for you, ready to review, waiting to install, working, scheduled, open, todo and done (todo and done start folded); items move between them on their own. Each row wears its area as a small tag. Press by group at the top to see your groups instead and drag between them; the choice holds on every device.

When claude asks typed questions (yes or no, pick one, pick many, rank, short or long text) the row shows one line, N questions, with an answer key. It opens a form with claude's recommendations marked: take one with its take recommendation key, or take all recommendations, add a note to any answer, and submit. Submit saves the answer and queues the tell like any other change. A plain reply on a typed ask is a comment: it does not answer the form.

In the swarm panel click an agent: its chat opens in a drawer on the right at the left drawer's width. Drag the drawer's left edge to resize it (the width is remembered on this device), press escape or the close key to shut it, or click another agent to swap it. The tasks viewer tab shows the huddle list of that one agent. A reply, add or tick is sent when you submit it: there is no send queue, and a tell to a busy agent shows as held until it is free.

Prototype, off by default: turn on channel delivery with PUT /api/v1/mcp-admin/channels {"enabled": true}; each NEW claude session then starts with a development-channels warning you answer in its pane, and a tell reaches it as a channel event instead of typed text (the answer says delivered_via channel or paste).

Open an item's move key and press fork...: pick a title and the fork's state (and, if you like, the original's), then fork. The new item is a copy beside the original and says where it came from; claude does the same with task_manager_fork.
Claude can flag an item with a color and a short reason (purple, pink, teal or lime): the row's left stripe wears that color and the status icon stays.
Open an item's move key and press move to todo to park it (the row reads todo and agents leave it alone unless you ask); take off todo brings it back.

Send something to the Task Manager and the browser keeps a copy until the server takes it: if the server hiccups the copy is sent again on its own, and the developer widget's sent tab can copy it or download all of them. The same tab lists your recent sends with when the agent was told (told, waiting to tell, held while its session is busy, read by the agent).

A task with subtasks (its forks) cannot be ticked until every subtask is done, and a task that still waits on its forks cannot be ticked at all: the tick stays empty and the list says why, naming each subtask and what it waits on. An agent cannot set such a task to review until each subtask is in review or done. Unticked review checks only warn.

catalog.description: Right of the usage meters in the terminal's bottom bar, a segment shows the running subagents and the open background shells and monitors (agents 2 bg 1), and a clock shows the live timer count and the time to the next fire. Both are drawn only when there is something to count, and neither is ever cut off: on a narrow bar the usage figures give way first, lowest priority first, and the segments shorten last (bg 3, 3·32m). Clicking a segment, or the bar, grows it into the session control center: the usage figures on the left, and on the right three lists. Scheduled tasks shows each timer's schedule, what it runs and when it next fires. Subagents shows the running ones with their type, task and age; a subagent runs inside claude, so its stop stops the background processes it started, and stop all interrupts the session with one escape, which stops the agent's current turn and every subagent in it. Background processes shows each tool shell's task, command summary, age and pid, with a stop per row and a stop all. Every stop asks first. The server only stops a process that is still the same process it listed and sits under that session's own agent: never the agent, never the pane's shell, never anything outside the session. Below 720px the two halves stack.
examples: A background ssh a subagent started hangs for hours: grow the bar, press stop on that subagent, and its shell is stopped without killing claude.
A runaway turn has three subagents fanned out: stop all over the subagents sends one escape and the whole turn stops.
On a 1024px cell the tokens figure now stays, because only the resets have to give way.

Press stop on a process row, or stop all over the list, read the question, then press the red answer; cancel or Escape backs out.

The context meter is a colored gauge: green, blue, yellow, orange, then red as the conversation fills, with the percent in the same color.

The model leads on the left, then the three limits (ctx, 5h, 7d) as one group; the timers segment sits on the right, drawn only when it has something to say; the agents and shells segments are off by default and appear there only once you turn them on in settings. The agents and shells numbers are exactly the lengths of the control center's AGENTS (running) and SHELLS lists.

Click the bar to grow it into the session control center, full width and never resizing the session: every figure as a labeled band across the top (context/model/tokens, the two windows, cost/account), with timers, agents and shells as three equal columns underneath, each with its own count and stop-all. On a phone the band becomes tiles and the three lists become an accordion, one section open at a time.

Which items the collapsed bar shows (model, effort, context, either rate-limit window, agents, shells, timers) can be turned on or off individually (agents and shells start off, the rest start on); the grown view always shows everything regardless.

Three layouts are built for the collapsed bar and three for the grown one, picked independently in settings (next to the status bar items list): collapsed A (meters first, default), B (a text status line grouped into session/account scopes) or C (attention-first, one meter for whichever limit is closest to its end); open A (a summary band plus three columns, default), B (a tabs rail: usage/timers/agents/shells) or C (one merged list grouped by owner, with filter chips).

examples: You remove a session and later find its transcript file is gone; restore the point from the session's conversation backups tab and resume the same conversation.
how_to: Turn on conversation backups (the save plugin) in plugins. It ships off; an install that already had it on keeps it on.

Conversation backups copy every conversation on disk into the backup vault when the plugin is turned on and keep it current as the conversation grows; killing, removing, sleeping or restarting a session also saves a point at that moment. A conversation whose file was later shortened or rewritten keeps the older point.
Open a session on the projects page and use its conversation backups tab, or GET /api/v1/cplugs/save/sessions/{session_uuid}/points; pin a point so it never ages out, or restore it.

A restore always puts the transcript back. Starting a session on it needs the permissions sessions.read and sessions.create, which you grant to the plugin on the plugins page; without them the tab tells you so in plain words.

Set how much disk conversation backups may use, and what they capture, in the plugin's settings pane on the plugins page (the storage slider and the capture scope: human, human and subsessions, or all; GET and PUT /api/v1/cplugs/save/settings and /capture-scope).

The vault never deletes a conversation's last copy, never deletes to get under the size limit, and tells you in the backup health alerts when it is over the limit, cannot be reached, has fallen behind, or holds conversations with no copy.

Choose where the vault lives in the plugin's settings pane (vault location, the setting vaultLocation; blank is the app data folder). A new location starts a new vault; nothing is moved and the old folder stays.

Plugin folders marked for the vault (the review boards and their drafts first) are backed up hourly into the same vault, git history included. GET /api/v1/cplugs/save/folders lists them with their size; POST /api/v1/cplugs/save/folders/{unit}/restore puts a copy in a new folder beside the original and never touches the original.

Old archive databases, recovered transcripts and the retired save store come in through POST /api/v1/cplugs/save/imports/preview (counts and a fingerprint, writes nothing) and POST /imports/apply (add only; undo with POST /imports/{run_id}/undo); an imported point shows an imported chip and its labels in the restore points table, and a junk, trash or review labeled import stays out of deep search until the once-over records a keep verdict.

catalog.description: Every widget this build carries, on the shared manager frame, as a places podium: a rail filters by group, by what fits a place and by state; a sticky podium of five places (right bar, bottom bar, drawer cards, glance row, dashboards) sits over the grouped widget cards, each with a live preview and marks for where it already is. A widget goes into a place by dragging its card onto the place, by the plus in the place's heading, or by the card's add button and its menu; a place can be picked to show only what fits it, and rows in a place reorder by drag or alt up and down and come out with remove, each with an undo toast. Opening a widget shows a reading pane: a live preview at the chosen size with sample or your own data, its views, a size switch (the chosen size in the accent, sizes it does not have greyed out), what it is, where it is placed, its generated options and an on and off toggle (green when on). Switching a widget off takes it out of every place. A widget that is off is no longer offered in any widgets menu. Fits is advice drawn from the sizes a widget declares; nothing is refused. Widgets are built into the app, so the page says plainly that none can be installed or removed here.
examples: Drag the activity log onto the right bar, then press undo in the toast if that was a mistake.
Pick the glance row to see which widgets can sit in it.
Switch off a widget you never use so it stops being offered and leaves every place it was in.
Turn off the activity log's system lines so it only shows what your sessions did.
how_to: Open the menu tab of the agents drawer and choose widgets.
Drag a widget card onto a place in the podium, or press the plus in a place's heading and pick a widget.
Press a place's name to show only the widgets that fit it; press it again to clear.
Press a card's add button, or its arrow to choose a place.
Press a card's name to open the reading pane; pick a size to see it drawn at that size.
In the pane, use the toggle to turn the widget off or on; use remove beside a place to take it out of that place.
In a place, drag a row to reorder it, or press alt and the up or down arrow; press the x to take it out.

catalog.description: Every configured launch wrapper on the shared manager frame, grouped by type (family), each group with a heading row that names the count and the type's default wrapper (or says there is none) and a plus that adds a wrapper of that type; each wrapper shows its family, the command it runs, the live sessions launched through it and its whole script. A wrapper's family and id are fixed once it exists - the id is also a launched session's stored agent type, so moving a wrapper to a different family would change what an already-launched session resolves to; add a new wrapper in the family you want instead. Export saves a wrapper as a small JSON file to share; import checks a shared file, shows its whole script, and writes only after you tick that you read it. An imported wrapper is never made a default. Each wrapper can wear its own icon, chosen with the shared icon picker in its detail pane; the same icon marks it in the new session menu and the restart and wake picker, and its share file carries it. The frame's own actions share it: export in the detail pane saves the file, remove takes away a wrapper that is not a default and that no live session runs through, after asking, and install in the title strip opens the reviewed import.
examples: Send a teammate your claude-chrome wrapper so their sessions launch with the same browser tools.
Check which live sessions still run through an old wrapper before you delete it in settings.
Give claude-chrome a globe so it stands out from your other claude wrappers when you start or restart a session.
